definition: Natural gas liquids (NGLs) are combustible hydrocarbons heavier than methane but lighter than naphtha/gasoline; they remain gaseous at standard temperature and pressure but liquefy more readily than methane than methane does. The five NGLs are ethane, propane, butane, iso-butane, and pentane.
core_idea: NGLs occupy the hydrocarbon weight range between methane (natural gas) and naphtha/gasoline, comprising five named compounds, and are commonly produced as a byproduct of natural gas processing and shale fracking.
key_points: NGLs are heavier than methane (natural gas) but light enough to remain gaseous at standard temperature and pressure.
NGLs are heavier than methane but lighter than naphtha/gasoline, and liquefy much more readily than methane.
The five NGLs are ethane (C2), propane (C3), butane (C4), iso-butane (IC4), and pentane (C5).
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) refers specifically to a mixture of the two heaviest common NGLs, propane and butane.
Pentanes mixed with slightly heavier hydrocarbons are called 'pentanes plus' or 'natural gasoline.'
NGLs are abundant in shale deposits and are a major byproduct of natural gas fracking.
relationships: NGLs sit between methane (natural gas) and naphtha/gasoline on the hydrocarbon weight spectrum
